newsitem.title: USA: GM unveils certified used vehicle program.
newsitem.headline: GM unveils certified used vehicle program.

text.p: General Motors Corp. formally unveiled its corporate GM Certified Used Vehicles plan Tuesday, touting the national programme as a way to give consumers more peace of mind when buying a used car.
GM cars and trucks that qualify for the programme will undergo a 110-point mechanical and cosmetic inspection and be sold at one, no-haggle price.

To be eligible, vehicles have to be from the last three model years and have 60,000 miles or less. The programme applies to Chevrolet, Buick, Oldsmobile, GMC and Pontiac vehicle lines. Cars sold by GM's Cadillac and Saturn divisions will continue to have their own separate used vehicle certification programmes.

Included in the purchase is a 12-month, 12,000-mile limited warranty, 24-hour roadside assistance and a three-day, 150-mile money-back guarantee. The terms are similar to programmes already offered by other automakers.

Among the Big Three, Ford Motor Co's Ford and Lincoln divisions, both have certification programmes. Chrysler Corp., is testing a programme in Kansas City, Mo., but has not decided if it will offer it on a national basis, said spokesman Mike McKesson.

About 500 of GM's 8,000 dealers have signed up to offer the certified vehicles. GM officials said they hope to have 700 by the end of this year. Dealers must pay $2,500 to enroll in the programme, which allows them to display special signage.

GM Certified vehicles may be sold alongside a dealer's other used cars, but they must be clearly marked. Some dealers, such as Jim Butler, a large GM dealer in the St. Louis area, have set up separate lots to handle the new GM Certified vehicles.
Jim Butler Certified Used Vehicles in Crestwood, Mo., was one of two dealerships that GM officials showcased during a media tour Tuesday.

GM's action comes as used car superstores are growing rapidly by offering customers a new, low-pressure buying experience. At the same time, many buyers are choosing used vehicles over more expensive new cars. The used vehicle market is expected to reach 42.3 million vehicles a year by 2000, about three times the size of the new vehicle market.
Because of the growth in new-car leasing, the number of low-mileage, high-quality used vehicles is also on the rise. It is expected to reach three million vehicles a year by 1999.
GM officials portrayed their programme as better than that of auto superstores, which GM said focus on the sales process and not the long-term experience.
"You don't need an 800-car lot and a cappuccino machine to sell used cars," said Roy Pikus, director of the GM Certified Used Vehicles programme.
A spokesman for Republic Industries Inc., which owns the AutoNation superstore chain, said GM's action is a sign that the AutoNation format is what consumers want.

"We're flattered that a company with the experience and brains that GM has has finally woken up to what customers have been asking for for 10 years, that we were the first to give," said spokesman Jim Donahue.
